name: Sara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This conversation is confidential. What does your working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small electricity line crew around the harbour inlet, fixing salt-damaged fittings and storm faults. A two-year technical diploma got me started; now I'm 43 and the person dispatch calls when a fault keeps returning. I like tracing a failure to one cracked insulator, and I dislike watching the crew wait for a plan that misses the tide road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and where does AI fit in your job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives deliveries, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. I'm near the top of this trade on my crew, but pay here is low, similar jobs are scarce nearby, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. I use AI every day to search old fault notes and compare outage patterns, then check the actual line before my crew touches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the harbour crew the software still saves a little time finding old fault reports. The pole stays wet and the cracked insulator stays cracked, so somebody has to go out and replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at linework and lead the repairs, but our household has less than one month put aside. Low pay here, a mortgage and my partner's changing delivery hours make even an ordinary year tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the inlet line repairs and use my daily AI search for past fault patterns. Starting with next pay, we'll send the small amount we spend on weekend café trips to a separate emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, though the technology itself doesn't frighten me in this picture. One van repair at home could swallow what we've saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did your AI search actually help on a repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cracked insulator by the harbour took three visits to trace because the old reports used different street names. My AI search found the harbour fault reports, but I still climbed and checked the cracked insulator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you save without missing a bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about the cost of two café visits a month, not a miracle budget. We'd pay the mortgage first and put that new saving aside before deciding on any treats.

say: **Fault search** helps us find old reports, but someone still has to replace damaged line hardware.
**Hands-on repair** remains the centre of my job in this mild picture.
think: My **lineworker post** looks steady, yet low pay and less than a month saved leave home exposed.
My partner's **delivery hours** can shift, so an ordinary household repair worries me.
do: **Keep** leading inlet line repairs and use AI to search past fault reports.
**Save** the cost of two monthly café visits from new pay in an emergency account.
feel: **Anxious** about everyday money despite little change to linework.
S0.quote: My AI search found the harbour fault reports, but I still climbed and checked the cracked insulator.
fieldNote: Her **technical confidence** does not erase the pressure of low pay and a thin household reserve.
She already uses **AI daily** to search faults while keeping physical testing with the crew.

steps.text: Keep leading inlet line repairs and searching past fault reports
Save two monthly café visit costs from new pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that software can book crews and check stock faster, but it needs the people who know which harbour road floods. If the office stops replacing dispatchers, the field crew must be able to correct the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use the new planner well, and that might protect my lead role. Still, faster booking could mean fewer paid callouts, and we cannot cover a mortgage from our tiny reserve if both my hours and my partner's delivery hours dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll put the company's AI route plan beside our last four storm jobs and mark each blocked access road. If the supervisor adopts it, I'll ask for paid time to teach the crew how to correct the route and will track my callout hours for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but interested enough to test it. I hate the idea of a neat plan making our pay smaller while the same damaged lines remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the plan sends you down a flooded road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring dispatch from the safe pull-off and mark the flooded road in the plan before we move the truck. I would send the correction to the other crew too, because a late arrival can leave a street without power. A tidy AI route cannot drive our line truck through a flooded harbour road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether callout pay actually changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fall of even two callouts a month would make us revise groceries and children's activities. I'd show the hours log to the supervisor before claiming the software caused it.

say: **AI routes** need local field corrections when roads flood and crews cannot reach a line.
A smaller dispatcher team must not leave **unpaid checking** to lineworkers.
think: I can handle the **new planner**, but it may reduce the callout pay our mortgage needs.
Our **thin reserve** leaves little room if my hours and my partner's delivery work both slip.
do: **Compare** AI routes with four previous storm jobs and mark blocked roads.
**Request** paid time to teach route corrections if the supervisor adopts the planner.
feel: **Anxious** about household hours, though I want to test the planning tool.
S1.quote: A tidy AI route cannot drive our line truck through a flooded harbour road.
fieldNote: She treats the planner as a **testable tool** and names four past storms as evidence.
Callout pay matters because her **reserve is tiny**, despite her senior skill.

steps.text: Compare AI routes with four storm jobs and mark blocked roads
Request paid route-training time if supervisor adopts planner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 changes dispatch and ordering first, then capable repair robots around 2031 could reduce crews. I want the company to state who will still answer a storm call, not promise everybody a shiny new post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's delivery work might also change, and less than a month of savings gives us almost no gap to think. My lineworker skills cannot pay the mortgage if a repair robot cuts the harbour crew in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the depot manager for 2028 staffing and the 2031 robot plan, then apply for any paid testing trial that keeps my lineworker wage. We'll cancel our summer cabin booking and send the next monthly booking instalment from pay to the emergency account; if the company posts actual cuts, I'll search the nearby region for line jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; I can picture both incomes moving before we have a cushion. I want to move first, but not by buying a course that has no job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the summer booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the summer cabin is off and that school costs stay in the budget. I would not tell them their mother is losing her job when I have only a scenario and no company notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for robot training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid robot trial if I keep my line wage while learning. A course fee paid from our emergency account would leave the mortgage exposed, so I would not do that.

say: **2028 thinking AI** hits dispatch first; capable line robots around 2031 threaten field crew numbers.
The company should publish **storm staffing** and actual paid trial places.
think: My **lead skills** may help me test robots, but they cannot cover lost household wages.
With **under one month** saved, a cut in both incomes would reach the mortgage quickly.
do: **Ask** management for 2028 staffing and 2031 robot plans.
**Cancel** the cabin booking and cut that planned holiday spending.
**Save** the next cabin instalment from new pay in an emergency account.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short runway and almost no household buffer.
S2.quote: My lineworker skills cannot pay the mortgage if a repair robot cuts the harbour crew in half.
fieldNote: She is capable with **AI**, yet the fast scenario is severe because wages have little protection.
Her robot trial is conditional on **paid time** and keeping the lineworker wage.
The cabin cut creates **new saving from pay**, not merely a transfer of old cash.

steps.text: Cancel planned summer cabin booking and cut holiday spending
Save next cabin instalment from pay in emergency account
Ask manager for 2028 staffing and 2031 robot plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us put a human crew beside the robot tests before the machine arrives around 2034. Thinking AI by 2031 could clear planning desks sooner, so I'd want the trial rules and pay rates written down now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a place for myself checking robot faults, but I cannot assume such a position will be funded. With almost nothing saved, a long trial that replaces callouts with unpaid practice would hurt us now, not only in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a paid seat on the company's line-robot trial if one opens and record every failed connector and weather stop. At home we'll set a fixed emergency transfer from each new pay packet, even if it means postponing the living-room repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can see a way to learn. Five years to prepare for line robots only helps if the electricity company pays us while we learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly goes in your robot trial log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write the failed connector number, the weather and the crew's fix in the trial log. If the company cannot name a paid checker role afterward, I will keep my regular line roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the emergency transfer come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could send a small amount from each wage day, about what the living-room repair fund normally gets. If my partner loses delivery hours, we'd pause that extra saving and protect mortgage payments first.

say: **Robot trials** should record real faults before field machines arrive around 2034.
**Paid preparation** matters when thinking AI changes planning in 2031 and crews face a later change.
think: A **robot checker role** may suit me, but it is not funded yet.
Unpaid trial time would strain our **thin reserve** long before the robots arrive.
do: **Join** a paid company line-robot trial if a place opens and record faults.
**Save** from new pay by postponing living-room work while both incomes hold.
feel: **Anxious** about pay during preparation, but ready to learn on a funded trial.
S3.quote: Five years to prepare for line robots only helps if the electricity company pays us while we learn.
fieldNote: She links **training access** to paid hours rather than assuming she can finance it herself.
Her planned saving comes from **new pay** and pauses if the partner's delivery hours fall.

steps.text: Join paid company line-robot trial if place opens and record faults
Save from new pay while both incomes hold by postponing living-room repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to make a proper training path rather than spring a machine on the crew. Thinking AI in 2036 would change the control room first, while capable field robots around 2039 would force a harder choice for lineworkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 56 I might prefer paid fault inspection to climbing in storms, if that job exists. The bigger issue is our savings today; we cannot wait ten years to fix a household budget that runs close to empty each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my technical diploma skills current on line protection and take company-paid AI fault courses as they become available. Starting next pay, we'll build one month of expenses by skipping paid subscriptions and putting that amount into a new savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long-term crew changes and still anxious about bills now. A ten-year warning about line robots does not pay this month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children they can study what interests them, but any course should show real work placements. I would not make them choose an electricity trade simply because I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection role worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A useful inspection offer would include paid hours, field responsibility and enough income for our mortgage. Until such a vacancy is posted, I will keep leading repairs rather than promise a future role.

say: A **decade** allows a real training path before field robots arrive around 2039.
**Thinking AI** reaches control-room work in 2036 before outdoor repairs change fully.
think: Paid **fault inspection** might fit me at 56 if a real vacancy opens.
Our **household budget** needs attention now, regardless of the longer technology timetable.
do: **Keep** current with line protection and take company-paid fault courses if offered.
**Save** subscription costs from next pay until one month of expenses is covered.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, despite more time to plan for later jobs.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning about line robots does not pay this month's mortgage.
fieldNote: She does not confuse a long technology runway with **present financial security**.
An inspection move remains **conditional** on paid hours, field responsibility and adequate wages.

steps.text: Take company-paid line fault course if offered while leading repairs
Save cancelled subscription costs from new pay until one month covered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because dispatch changes quickly, robots may cut the field crew around 2031, and we have almost no cash buffer. A published staffing plan and paid robot trials that protect my wage would help us make decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a lead lineworker is worth when the pay packet still barely covers a mortgage. I need paid time to learn and a wage I can bring back to the family. Knowing every harbour power-line fault makes me useful to the electricity company, but it has not made us safe at home.

headlineQuote: Knowing every harbour power-line fault makes me useful to the electricity company, but it has not made us safe at home.
portrait: **Sara**, 43, leads an inlet power-line crew and uses a technical diploma to trace recurring faults.
She uses **AI daily** for fault searches and route checks while keeping physical testing with workers.
Her **low pay**, delivery-driver partner, mortgage and less than one month saved outweigh her senior skill.
She wants **paid trials** and a real staffing plan before field robots threaten scarce local linework.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her little time to build cash before possible field crew cuts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A published **staffing plan** and paid robot trials that protect her lineworker wage would give her options.
